ai_text: It sounds like the TA responsibility has added another layer to an already busy routine. You want to do the job properly, but your own work still needs your attention too.

user_text: Yes. I don't want to be careless with the students.
ai_text: That concern actually shows that you're taking the responsibility seriously. Wanting your students to get proper support is a good quality in a TA.

user_text: But sometimes I don't know how much I should help them.
ai_text: Are you mainly unsure about how much time to spend with each student, or about how much of their problem you should solve for them?

user_text: Both, especially when several students ask me questions at the same time.
ai_text: That can be difficult for a new TA. When several students need help together, it's usually better to prioritize common problems first and then handle individual issues one by one rather than trying to solve everything simultaneously.

user_text: Sometimes I feel that if I don't answer everyone immediately, I'm not doing my job properly.
ai_text: Not answering immediately doesn't mean you're neglecting them. Being responsible also means managing your attention so you can give useful answers instead of rushing through everyone's questions.

user_text: I think I put too much pressure on myself.
ai_text: It sounds like the expectations you're placing on yourself may be higher than what the role actually requires. You can care about the students without having to be available for every problem at every moment.

user_text: But I also have my research work and other things to finish.
ai_text: That's an important part of the situation. Your TA work is one responsibility, not your entire academic role. Protecting time for your own research isn't selfish; it's necessary if you're going to manage everything sustainably.

user_text: Then how should I divide my time?
ai_text: You could set specific periods for TA-related work, keep a separate block for research, and avoid switching between them constantly. We can also make a simple priority list for tasks that genuinely need your attention today versus those that can wait.

user_text: I think constantly switching between tasks is making me more tired.
ai_text: That makes sense. Switching repeatedly forces your attention to restart each time. Grouping similar tasks together could reduce that mental load and help you feel more in control.

user_text: I still want the students to feel that they can approach me when they need help.
ai_text: You can keep that accessibility without being available constantly. For example, you could establish a clear time for questions or encourage students to collect related doubts before approaching you.

user_text: I guess I need to find a balance instead of trying to do everything perfectly.
ai_text: Exactly. You don't have to become a perfect TA immediately. Give yourself some time to understand the role, set reasonable boundaries, and keep enough space for rest and your own work. With experience, this will likely feel much more manageable.
